en: The Buddha spoke this sutra on receiving retribution in the present life concerning a certain woman who was traveling alone without a companion.
He then asked her, "Sister, for what reason is your countenance so lovely and yet so withered? What is it that afflicts you? At that time, the woman replied:
I am of meager merit;
having married this husband,
I hoped we would protect and preserve one another.
Unexpectedly, I fell ill and died one day.
My family members took me and buried me alive in a tomb,
where I remained for a full seven days.
A band of robbers plundered this tomb,
seeking its treasures;
they have taken me back to their home.
He took her as his wife.
Later, the bandit leader plundered a village and was killed by another.
They gathered the remains and performed the encoffining and burial;
my relatives escorted me.
Furthermore, he was buried alive for three full days,
after which he again became a wild fox.
Desiring to devour a corpse,
he came to defile this tomb;
because of this, I was able to escape.
The parents and their retinue were unaware of this.
At that time, the elder’s son spoke to the woman, saying,
"My wife has only just died."
"Since you have no husband,
shall we two now become husband and wife? Can you do this?"
At that time, the woman had no other destination and immediately consented;
they followed one another until they reached her home.
They cherished one another with mutual affection;
thus, after exactly one year, a son was born,
and at a later time, yet another son was born.
Furthermore, at a later time, she became pregnant again.
When her month was near and she was about to give birth,
the elder’s son went out on a journey.
He gathered with his companions for a drinking party and returned at dusk;
his wife then firmly bolted the doors from within.
While she remained on the ground giving birth,
blood and fluids were scattered in disarray;
the husband returned and called out to his wife.
His wife, having given birth, remained crouching on the ground;
with blood and afterbirth scattered in disarray,
she was unable to open the door.
When he called out but received no response,
he drew his sword, broke down the door,
and immediately questioned his wife.
"I went out this morning;
when I was about to return, I called for you,
but you did not answer as the gate was closed."
"What difference is there in my feelings?
The wife replied to her husband,
"It is because of giving birth to a child that blood and fluids have been scattered in disarray."
The husband said to his wife,
"Where is the son we have borne now?
His wife then immediately brought the son she had borne and presented him to her husband.
Upon obtaining this child, he immediately boiled it with fresh butter and restricted his wife to eating it; however,
the wife could not bear to eat it.
He immediately drew a sharp sword, intending to take his life;
however, out of a craving for life, the wife then ate her son until he was entirely consumed.
When her husband awoke from his intoxication at dawn the following morning,
he immediately asked his wife,
"I returned home yesterday at night."
"Being intoxicated and mentally confused, there should be no fault.
The wife replied to her husband,
"You returned home last night in a state of darkness."
He called out for me to open the door.
Because I had given birth at an improper time, I did not open the door.
You hacked at the door and entered, and immediately questioned me.
"What difference is there in feeling?
I replied to you:
"It is for the sake of producing offspring that blood and fluids flow in profusion."
"If you seek from me the child born of me,
I shall grant him to you.
Once you have obtained this child, you may immediately boil him with ghee."
"You have restricted me to eating this;
I cannot bear to eat it.
The man then drew his sword and intended to kill me.
"Out of greed for my own life, I have devoured my children until they were all gone.
When her husband heard these words,
he immediately bowed his head.
Feeling extreme shame and remorse,
he apologized to his wife for the transgression of being intoxicated.
"I pray that you do not harbor resentment.
From this day forward, I vow never to drink alcohol.
Later, at another time, his wife spoke to her husband.
Since I have been separated from my parents,
years and months have passed without word of their whereabouts.
As for the two of us and our two children—
He went to his parents' house to pay his respects and inquire after their welfare.
At that time, the elder’s son, together with his wife and two sons, set out along the road;
they encountered the scorching heat of the day.
Her husband immediately stopped under a tree;
seeking shade to avoid the heat, he fell fast asleep.
Suddenly, he was bitten by a black snake and died instantly.
His wife wept and,
taking her two children in her arms, immediately set out on the road ahead.
She encountered a water pit.
The elder son was in urgent distress and could not be rescued.
After the light had escorted the elder son to the shore,
he then intended to turn back and retrieve the younger son.
Upon seeing his mother, the son immediately rushed toward the water and was submerged by the waves;
he then came back onto the shore, wishing to embrace his elder brother.
She was immediately devoured by tigers and wolves.
At that time, the woman cried out to heaven and called upon the earth,
lamenting, "What evil karma have I committed that I now encounter such suffering?"
Even as he proceeded forward to see his parents' home,
the acquaintances in the village asked him,
"Have you seen my parents, brothers, and kinsmen; are they all in peace?"
The man of knowledge replied,
"A fire broke out in your house;
everyone, both great and small, has been burned to death by the flames, and there is no one left."
When the woman heard this,
she fainted once more and was unable to move.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the great assembly.
He immediately observed this woman with his divine eye and said to Ānanda:
"Take this precious robe and go to meet this woman."
Ānanda, having received these instructions, went forth with the precious robe to welcome this woman.
Upon arriving among the assembly,
she paid homage to the World-Honored One.
Feeling shame and remorse, he repented.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him;
he severed all fetters and outflows, attaining the fruit of Arhatship.
The Buddha again addressed the entire assembly:
"If you wish to know the good and evil deeds of this woman in her previous lives,
listen attentively and reflect upon them well."
Be careful not to forget this.
Long ago, in incalculable kalpas past, there was the son of a householder whose wealth was immeasurable.
He took a wife,
but after a full year had passed, they still had no children.
At that time, the elder’s son reflected to himself:
I now possess great wealth but have no son;
were I to pass away suddenly, there would be no one to whom my property could be entrusted.
Subsequently, I took a concubine.
Within one year of her marriage, she gave birth to a son whose countenance was handsome and upright;
the elder brother took pity on him.
At that time, the senior wife reflected to herself:
"I am the senior wife, yet I have no son;
it has not been many years since I first took this concubine."
"Since I have given birth to a son,
when he grows up, the wealth shall belong to him;
I will certainly be cast aside and treated with contempt by my husband."
"I ought now to devise some stratagem to kill this child.
At that time, the mother of the concubine was away and not at home;
the principal wife, having settled her plan within the house, immediately used two iron needles to pierce the child's cheeks.
The young child cried out in pain that was beyond description;
his mother held him, not knowing where the pain lay,
calling out to heaven and crying to the earth.
"If there be anyone with an evil mind, a mind of anger, a mind of malice, or a mind of envy who kills my son,
may they suffer the retribution of pain in birth after birth throughout all their lives.
At that time, the senior wife’s mind became naturally clear and pure.
She immediately stood before her husband and her concubine and made this oath:
"If I, with an evil mind, a mind of anger, a mind of jealousy, or a mind of envy, should kill your son,
may I receive a female body again in birth after birth throughout all my future lives."
Having married her husband, she buried him alive in a tomb and vowed:
"In every life and every age, should I give birth to a son,
I shall boil him with fresh butter and eat him."
May it be that in every lifetime and birth, my husband is bitten by a snake,
my son is swept away by water, and my child is devoured by a tiger;
may the entire family, both great and small, be utterly consumed and killed by fire.
When the curse had been completed, the son died immediately.
At that time, the senior wife, reflecting within her heart with a sense of purity, established this oath:
"May there be no separation between sin and merit, just as a shadow follows a form, never forsaking one another."
Furthermore, for five hundred lifetimes, this principal wife abandoned one body and took up another,
constantly undergoing the retribution of suffering.
The Buddha then addressed the entire great assembly:
I shall now explain for you:
what merit did this woman cultivate in her previous lives that she has encountered me once again?
He covered her with his robe and preached the Dharma for her;
when she severed all fetters and outflows and attained the path of Arhatship,
it was because this woman, during immeasurable kalpas in the past, [had cultivated roots of goodness].
The family was extremely poor.
There was a pratyekabuddha who converted them through his teaching.
This woman had no money,
so she untied her sash and gave it to the pratyekabuddha.
By virtue of this cause and condition, she was born beautiful and always into wealthy families.
Although he underwent such suffering as before for five hundred lifetimes, he again encountered me;
I covered him with my robe,
preached the Dharma for him, and enabled him to sever all fetters and outflows, attaining the path of Arhatship.
"Even though they have attained the Way, they must constantly endure the suffering of hot iron for six periods every day;
it enters through the crown of their heads and pierces to their hearts.
The Buddha then addressed the entire great assembly once more.
From this day forward, be careful not to harbor evil thoughts, anger, or envy.
Do not further harm one another or cast curses upon one another.
Speak thus: "There is no karmic retribution; it follows one like a shadow follows a form, and shall never be abandoned."
Whether one performs good or evil deeds, one receives the retribution for evil; ultimately, there is no self that acts while another receives the reward.
Although the body perishes, good and evil do not decay.
As has been explained above, you should receive and uphold this with careful attention.
At that time, the great assembly, as well as the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of spirits, and those among the ghosts and deities who harbored evil intentions,
all conceived thoughts of loving-kindness.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, they received and upheld it with profound reverence.
The Scripture on the Buddha’s Teaching that One Shall Receive Immediate Retribution, in one fascicle.
